one_liner: RISC-V to x86-64 user-mode JIT binary translator; its 2017 paper shows about 1.8x faster than QEMU riscv64 user mode.
what_it_does: rv8 is a suite of RISC-V tools for x86-64 hosts. rv-jit runs static RISC-V Linux ELF binaries (RV32/RV64 IMAFDC) by proxying a small set of Linux system calls to the host. rv-sim is the interpreter-only proxy simulator, rv-sys an interpreted full-system emulator for the 1.9.1 privileged spec, and rv-bin and rv-meta handle ELF dumps, histograms and ISA metadata. You use it like qemu-riscv64 (`rv-jit <elf>`), not as a library: the JIT has no public embedding API (issue #15 is still open). It runs only static binaries, with no dynamic linking (#58).
how_it_is_fast: It starts as an interpreter that profiles for hot paths; after a trace runs a set number of times (trace_iters, default 100), it records the path through calls and emits x86-64 code with AsmJit. Register mapping is static: twelve hot RISC-V registers (chosen from dynamic profiles) live in fixed x86-64 registers, and the rest sit in a spill area at [rbp+off] that instructions use directly as CISC memory operands. Hot callees are inlined, with a compare-against-expected-return check. Indirect jumps go through a 1024-entry direct-mapped jump-target cache, and branch-tail trampolines are relinked lazily once their target is translated. Macro-op fusion turns common RISC-V idioms into single x86 instructions (AUIPC+ADDI into MOV, SLLI/SRLI 32 into MOVZX, shift/shift/OR into ROR). Guest loads and stores are emitted as plain host memory accesses at the guest address, with no MMU call or bounds check.
when_to_use: Studying or teaching dynamic binary translation: the RV64 emitter (src/jit/jit-emitter-rv64.h, about 4,300 lines) and the CARRV 2017 paper show static register mapping, trace inlining and macro-op fusion in compact form
Running integer-heavy, statically linked RV64 or RV32 Linux binaries (musl static builds like rv8-bench's) on an x86-64 Linux or macOS host, faster than the 2017-era QEMU riscv64 user mode
Prototyping new fusion patterns or register-allocation ideas for RISC-V-on-x86 translation, where a small codebase matters more than ISA coverage
Generating RISC-V opcode maps, LaTeX listings, decoders or instruction histograms with rv-meta and rv-bin
when_not_to_use: Floating-point or atomic-heavy guests: only the base integer and M instructions are JIT-compiled, while F, D and A fall back to the interpreter (README; issues #32 and #34 are still open). Every benchmark behind the speed claim is integer-only
Dynamically linked, glibc or multithreaded programs, or programs that need more than a small set of Linux syscalls: rv-jit supports static ELF only (#58) and ioctl is a stub (#49)
Isolating untrusted guest code: the JIT shares one address space with the emulator and emits unchecked host loads and stores, so it is not a sandbox
Current RISC-V software: the target is the 1.9.1 privileged-spec era (no V, B/Zb*, or other later extensions), the only JIT host is x86-64, and there are no commits since 2018
Anything that needs a maintained emulator against a current QEMU: the only head-to-head data uses the 2017 riscv/riscv-qemu fork, and QEMU's RISC-V TCG has been upstream and improved since

integration.form: command-line executables (rv-jit, rv-sim, rv-sys, rv-bin, rv-meta) plus internal static libraries (libriscv_asm.a, libriscv_elf.a, libriscv_gen.a, libriscv_model.a, libriscv_util.a); GNU make build
integration.dependencies: git submodules: an AsmJit fork (michaeljclark/asmjit, old asmjit/base API) and riscv-meta; uses google::dense_hash_map; a RISC-V GNU toolchain (RISCV env var) is needed to build the test programs
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (-std=c++1y, -fno-rtti -fno-exceptions, default -O3 -fwrapv). README: gcc 5.4 or clang 3.4 minimum, gcc 6.3 or clang 3.8 recommended. GCC 11.4 fails to build without adding #include <limits> (issue #68, open)
integration.platforms: Host: x86-64 only (Linux, macOS; FreeBSD 11 listed as alpha). The host CPU needs RDTSCP (src/util/host.h); issue #48 reports 'illegal hardware instruction' on a Core 2 Duo. Guests: RV32IMAFDC and RV64IMAFDC, privileged ISA 1.9.1
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The JIT run loop registers itself as a process-wide singleton (jit_singleton::current) and installs process-wide signal handlers, so plan on one emulated hart per process.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: `rv-jit <elf>` replaces `qemu-riscv64 <elf>` only for static, single-image binaries that use rv8's small proxy-syscall set; no dynamic linking, and only the IM subset is JIT-compiled

gotchas: Harness flaw: rv8-bench.js counts a run as valid when the exit status is 0 and never checks program output, so the measurements never showed that rv8 computed correct results. The benchmark sources also have bugs. primes.c shifts an int 1 by up to 63 bits (undefined behaviour, so the sieve depends on how the compiler lowers it). qsort.c's comparator `*ia - *ib` overflows on the full-range ints it generates. norx.c's tag check is inverted and main zeroes the tag before decrypting. aes.c and norx.c print their memcmp result but always return 0. The rv8-vs-QEMU comparison stays valid because both run the same riscv64 binary, but native-vs-guest ratios rest on different compilations of UB-laden code.
Native x86-64 reference runs are launched under `perf stat`, so perf startup is inside the native wall time. This affects only the ratios to native, not rv8 vs QEMU.

The JIT's use_mmu flag is never set, so the MMU-call load/store path is dead code. Translated code reads and writes host memory directly at guest addresses in an identity-mapped shared address space (MAP_FIXED at the ELF's vaddr). By default it does not update instret (needs -i). fence.i flushes the whole trace cache.

In the paper's summary table the two QEMU columns are swapped relative to Figures 9 and 10. Its '75% faster than the leading competitor' compares rv8 with QEMU aarch64 running aarch64 builds; against QEMU riscv64 the -O3 gap is 1.79x. Also, the riscv-qemu build line in rv8-bench's README configures only the softmmu targets, not the qemu-riscv64 user-mode binary the harness invokes.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick rv8 only to study or extend a compact RISC-V-to-x86-64 translator built around static register mapping and macro-op fusion. For maintained RISC-V emulation pick libriscv (embeddable, sandboxed), rv32emu (RV32, benchmarked against QEMU v9.0.0) or RVVM (full-system RV64), all of which are active, unlike rv8.
verified_claims_summary: In the authors' peer-reviewed CARRV 2017 paper, seven integer rv8-bench programs (aes, dhrystone, miniz, norx, primes, qsort, sha512; riscv64, GCC 7.2.0 and musl, static -fPIE, best of 20 runs) have a geomean runtime of 2.62x native x86-64 under rv8 at -O3, against 4.68x for 2017 riscv-qemu user mode (about 1.79x faster, derived from page data) and 4.57x for QEMU aarch64. At -Os the figures are 2.47x vs 4.62x (about 1.87x). rv8 is slightly slower than QEMU riscv64 on norx at -O3 (1.20 s vs 1.17 s). The host (Core i7-5557U Broadwell) is named only in rv8-bench's results template, not in the paper. A 2018 independent study ('Towards a High-Performance RISC-V Emulator', search snippet only, paper not opened) reports average MiBench slowdowns of 3.16x for rv8 and 7.07x for QEMU.
status_note: Abandoned: last commit 2018-09-22, the repo now sits under larkmjc (the michaeljclark URL redirects), 42 open issues, and GCC 11+ needs a one-line <limits> patch to build. It is MIT-licensed, but the LICENSE file has no copyright line (issue #61), so it is usable for study and vendoring, not production.
